proc-start-dreaded-task.title: Starting the task I’ve been avoiding for weeks
proc-start-dreaded-task.line: I open the thing I’ve been dreading and do the first piece before I can talk myself out of it.

fixes.title: Set a timer for 25 minutes and stop when it rings
fixes.whatChanges: Francesco Cirillo came up with this as a university student in the late 1980s, using a kitchen timer shaped like a tomato. Agreeing to only 25 minutes makes the start much smaller, and you’re allowed to quit when the timer goes off.
fixes.firstStep: Pick the task, set a 25-minute timer on your phone, and open the file or envelope.

fixes.title: Decide exactly when and where you’ll start
fixes.whatChanges: Psychologists call this an if-then plan, such as opening the letter from the insurance company at the kitchen table at 9am tomorrow. A 2006 review by Gollwitzer and Sheeran found that plans this specific helped people follow through, though a later review found a smaller effect.
fixes.firstStep: Write one sentence that says when, where and the first thing you’ll do.
fixes.featureIdea: Helps you write one sentence saying when, where and the first thing you'll do on a task you're avoiding, then checks in at that time to ask how it went.

fixes.title: Block the websites you escape to
fixes.whatChanges: Apps like Freedom block the sites and apps you choose on your phone and computer at the same time, so the easy way out isn’t there. The basic version is free, and the full one costs $39.99 a year.
fixes.firstStep: List the three sites you open first when you’re avoiding something, and block them for one hour.

proc-feeling-behind-it.title: Understanding the feeling that makes me put things off
proc-feeling-behind-it.line: When I notice I’m avoiding something, I can name what it makes me feel and still take the first step.

fixes.title: Name the feeling the task brings up
fixes.whatChanges: The psychologists Sirois and Pychyl argued in 2013 that putting things off is mostly about getting away from a bad feeling right now, like boredom, worry or self-doubt, rather than a lack of willpower. Knowing which feeling you’re dodging often tells you what would make the task easier, such as company for a boring job or a second opinion for a scary one.
fixes.firstStep: Write the task down, and next to it write the one word for how it makes you feel.
fixes.featureIdea: Asks you to name in one word how a stalled task makes you feel before you start, then suggests a small first step that fits that feeling.

fixes.title: Forgive yourself for the last time you put it off
fixes.whatChanges: In a 2010 study of 134 first-year college students, the ones who forgave themselves for putting off studying for their first exams put off studying less before the next round. Being hard on yourself tends to make the task feel worse, and the students who went easier on themselves did better.
fixes.firstStep: Say or write one sentence letting yourself off the hook for the last delay, then look at what’s next.
fixes.featureIdea: Helps you write one sentence letting yourself off the hook for the last delay, then turns your attention to the next step.

proc-stuck-next-step.title: Knowing the next step on a stuck task
proc-stuck-next-step.line: When a project stalls, I can see the one small action that will get it moving again.

fixes.title: Write down the next physical action, not the whole project
fixes.whatChanges: David Allen’s Getting Things Done method rests on this idea: “do taxes” is a project, while “find last year’s tax form in the file drawer” is something you can start. Many tasks stay stuck because the first concrete step was never named.
fixes.firstStep: Pick one stalled task and write the very next thing you’d physically do, starting with a verb.
fixes.featureIdea: Helps you turn a stalled project into the very next physical action, starting with a verb, and nudges you when what you wrote is still a project.

fixes.title: Ask for the thing you’re waiting on
fixes.whatChanges: Sometimes a task is stalled because you’re waiting on a form, an answer or a decision from someone else, and it quietly sits on your list as if it were your fault. Sending one short message to ask for what you need is often the whole step.
fixes.who: You and whoever you’re waiting on
fixes.firstStep: Send one message today asking for the thing you’re waiting on, with a date you need it by.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Common practice; no source was opened for this.

proc-work-alongside-someone.title: Getting boring tasks done with someone else there
proc-work-alongside-someone.line: I sit down with a friend, or on a video call with a stranger, and we both get through the tasks we’ve been avoiding.

fixes.title: Do your task while a friend does theirs
fixes.whatChanges: Having another person nearby, even one doing something completely different, can make it easier to stay with a dull or uncomfortable task. An ADHD coach named this body doubling, and people without ADHD use it too.
fixes.firstStep: Text a friend and ask if they’d like to spend an hour this week working on your own lists side by side.

fixes.title: Book a video work session with a stranger
fixes.whatChanges: Focusmate pairs you on video with another person for 25, 50, or 75 minutes: you each say what you’ll work on, work quietly, and check in at the end. Three sessions a week are free.
fixes.firstStep: Book one 25-minute session for the task you’ve been putting off longest.

fixes.title: Put money on a deadline with a friend as referee
fixes.whatChanges: On stickK, a site started in 2008 by two Yale economists, you set a goal, pick a friend to confirm whether you did it, and put money on it that goes elsewhere if you miss. The co-founder reported that 78% of people who used both money and a referee reached their goal, compared with 35% of those who put no money down.
fixes.firstStep: Choose one task, a date, and a friend you’d trust to say honestly whether you did it.

proc-drop-what-doesnt-matter.title: Letting go of tasks I don’t actually need to do
proc-drop-what-doesnt-matter.line: I’ve stopped carrying around tasks I was never going to do, and the ones left on my list are ones I mean.

fixes.title: Cross off a task you’ve already decided against
fixes.whatChanges: A task that has sat on the list for months is sometimes one you’ve quietly decided not to do. Crossing it off on purpose frees up the attention it keeps taking every time you see it.
fixes.firstStep: Read your to-do list and cross off one item you’ve kept for months and don’t want to do.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Common practice; no source was opened for this.

fixes.title: Flip a coin on a decision you’ve put off for months
fixes.whatChanges: In a study published in 2021, the economist Steven Levitt had people who were stuck on a big decision, like quitting a job or a class, let a coin toss guide them. Those the coin told to make the change were happier six months later than those it told to stay put.
fixes.firstStep: Write the decision as a yes-or-no question, flip a coin, and notice whether you feel relieved or disappointed.

fixes.title: Pay or trade someone to do a task you dread
fixes.whatChanges: If a task matters but you’ve dreaded it for a year, someone else can often do it for a fee or a trade, like a tax preparer, a handyman, or a friend who enjoys paperwork. Paying for it is a reasonable trade when the dread has been costing you for months.
fixes.who: You and someone you hire or trade with
fixes.firstStep: Write down one task you’d happily pay to never think about again, and look up what it would cost.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Common practice; no source was opened for this.

proc-check-for-adhd.title: Finding out whether ADHD is part of the picture
proc-check-for-adhd.line: I know whether something like ADHD is behind my trouble getting started, and I’m getting the right kind of help for it.

fixes.title: Fill out a six-question checklist about focus and follow-through
fixes.whatChanges: Researchers working with the World Health Organization wrote a six-question checklist that adults can fill out about common ADHD signs. A high score isn’t a diagnosis; it’s something to bring to a doctor.
fixes.firstStep: Answer the six questions honestly about the last six months and save your answers.

fixes.title: Ask your doctor about an ADHD evaluation
fixes.whatChanges: The National Institute of Mental Health notes that ADHD usually starts in childhood and often continues into adulthood, so many people first learn they have it as adults. A doctor can do an evaluation or refer you to someone who does, and the answer either way tells you which fixes are worth your time.
fixes.firstStep: Write down three recent examples of things you meant to do and didn’t, to bring to your appointment.

fixes.title: Look up an ADHD specialist near you or online
fixes.whatChanges: CHADD, a national ADHD nonprofit, keeps a free directory of hundreds of clinicians, coaches and clinics that you can search by state, profession and whether they see people remotely.
fixes.firstStep: Search the directory for your state and save the names of two people who see adults.

proc-work-fits-attention.title: A job set up around how my attention works
proc-work-fits-attention.line: At work I get tasks in writing, a short weekly check-in, and reminders, so things I’m responsible for don’t slip.

fixes.title: Ask a free advice service what changes to request at work
fixes.whatChanges: The Job Accommodation Network gives free, confidential advice on changes at work, and its ADHD list includes to-do lists, help setting priorities, a mentor, and timers or calendar apps. The network can also explain how the Americans with Disabilities Act applies to your job.
fixes.firstStep: Read the network’s ADHD page and circle the two changes that would make the most difference to you.

fixes.title: Ask your manager for written tasks and a weekly check-in
fixes.whatChanges: Two of the simplest items on the Job Accommodation Network’s list cost an employer nothing: getting tasks in writing and a short weekly meeting to agree on what comes first. You don’t need a diagnosis to ask for either.
fixes.firstStep: Ask your manager for a 15-minute weekly check-in on priorities, starting next week.

proc-understand-my-pattern.title: Understanding which kind of putting off I’m doing
proc-understand-my-pattern.line: I can tell whether I’m avoiding a feeling, stuck on a step, holding a task I don’t want, or dealing with something like ADHD, and I know what to try for each.

fixes.title: Sort the tasks you’ve put off by why they’re stuck
fixes.whatChanges: Walks you through a few questions about each task you’ve been putting off: does it bring up a feeling, is it waiting on someone, do you still want it done, and does this happen with almost everything. Each answer points to a different kind of fix, drawing on research like Sirois and Pychyl’s, without pretending to diagnose you.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this, and write down the three tasks you’ve put off longest.

fixes.title: Keep a private log of what you put off
fixes.whatChanges: Keeps a simple log, on your device, of what you put off and what finally got it moving, so after a few weeks you can see whether it’s mostly phone calls, paperwork, or nearly everything. That pattern is useful for you and for a doctor if you decide to see one.
fixes.firstStep: For the next week, jot down each thing you put off and what you did instead.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Proposed It feature; no source for this kind of log was opened in this run.

fixes.title: Bring a clear summary to your doctor
fixes.whatChanges: Helps you put together a short list of real examples to take to a doctor, if the pattern shows up at work, with bills and at home over many years. The National Institute of Mental Health describes ADHD as starting in childhood, so examples from school help too.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this, and write down one example from school and one from this month.

proc-weekly-work-hour.title: A regular weekly hour to work alongside neighbors
proc-weekly-work-hour.line: Every week I go to the same table at the library with a few other people, and the things I’ve been putting off get done there.

fixes.title: Go to a free quiet work session
fixes.whatChanges: Shut Up & Write runs free sessions in more than 80 countries, in cafés, libraries, and online: you say what you’re working on, work quietly together, and check in at the end. Nobody reads your work or comments on it, so bills and emails are as welcome as novels.
fixes.firstStep: Look up the nearest session, in person or online, and put the next one on your calendar.

fixes.title: Start a weekly work hour at your library or café
fixes.whatChanges: If there isn’t a session near you, two or three people and a regular time are enough, using the same simple Shut Up & Write format with no teacher and no feedback.
fixes.firstStep: Pick a time and place, then invite two people you know who also have things they’ve been putting off.

fixes.title: Find neighbors who want a regular work session
fixes.whatChanges: Matches people nearby who want to work side by side at a set time and place, the way Focusmate pairs strangers online.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this, and note which day and time would suit you.

proc-split-big-deadline.title: Turning one far-off deadline into several near ones
proc-split-big-deadline.line: My big projects have in-between dates I actually meet, so the final week isn’t a panic.

fixes.title: Put three in-between dates on your calendar
fixes.whatChanges: A deadline months away is easy to ignore, because nothing happens today if you skip it. Breaking it into a draft date, a check date, and a done date gives you a near deadline almost every week.
fixes.firstStep: Open your calendar and mark three dates between now and your real deadline, each with what’s due.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Common practice; the best-known study on self-set deadlines (Ariely and Wertenbroch, 2002) failed to replicate, so it is not cited.

fixes.title: Tell one person your first in-between date
fixes.whatChanges: A date only you know about is easy to move. Telling a friend or coworker, and asking them to check in that day, turns it into something you’ve agreed to.
fixes.who: You and a friend or coworker
fixes.firstStep: Message one person your first in-between date and ask them to check in on it.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Common practice; no source was opened for this.

proc-household-paperwork.title: Sharing the household tasks that keep getting put off
proc-household-paperwork.line: My partner and I each handle the chores and bills we mind least, so nothing sits for months.

fixes.title: Swap a dreaded task with someone who doesn’t mind it
fixes.whatChanges: One person’s dreaded phone call is another person’s five-minute errand. Trading tasks you each hate for ones you don’t mind is a simple way to get both done.
fixes.who: You and your partner, roommate, or family
fixes.firstStep: Each of you list the three household tasks you put off most, then trade one.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Household practice; no source was opened for this.

fixes.title: Hold a monthly paperwork hour together
fixes.whatChanges: Sitting down together once a month for bills, forms, and appointments means nobody faces the pile alone. Picking a set day, like the first Sunday of the month, keeps it from becoming another thing to schedule.
fixes.firstStep: Pick a date this month and put a one-hour paperwork session on the shared calendar.
fixes.speculativeRationale: Household practice; no source was opened for this.

proc-forms-fill-themselves.title: Tax forms that come already filled in
proc-forms-fill-themselves.line: My tax return arrives pre-filled from what my employer and bank already reported, so all I do is check it and approve.

fixes.title: Push for tax returns the government fills in for you
fixes.whatChanges: In Sweden, the tax agency fills in your return from what employers and banks already reported, and if nothing needs changing you can approve it online, by text or by phone. Some people want the same where they live, while tax-prep companies and others argue against a bigger government role.
fixes.who: Voters, lawmakers, and the tax agency
fixes.firstStep: Read how the Swedish Tax Agency describes approving a return, so you can explain the idea to someone else.

fixes.title: Weigh in on filing taxes directly with the government for free
fixes.whatChanges: In 2024 the IRS ran a pilot called Direct File in 12 states, and 140,803 people filed their federal taxes directly with the government for free. Of the users surveyed, 90% rated it excellent or above average, though the program has been politically contested.
fixes.firstStep: Look up whether your state took part and what your members of Congress have said about it.

fixes.title: Tell your representatives what you think about pre-filled taxes
fixes.whatChanges: Helps you find your representatives and send a short note in your own words, for or against free and pre-filled filing, with the Direct File pilot results attached.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this, and write two sentences about what tax season is like for you.

proc-reminders-before-deadlines.title: A clear reminder before deadlines that cost me to miss
proc-reminders-before-deadlines.line: Before a court date, renewal or benefits deadline, I get a reminder that says when, where and what happens if I miss it.

fixes.title: Ask your city or county for plain text reminders
fixes.whatChanges: In New York City in 2018, text reminders that explained the consequences and asked people to plan how they’d get there cut missed court dates by 26%, and with a redesigned summons form the drop was 36%. Many missed dates are simply forgotten, and a better reminder is cheap to send.
fixes.firstStep: Check whether your county court or motor vehicle office offers text reminders, and sign up if it does.

fixes.title: Get reminders for every deadline with a penalty
fixes.whatChanges: Keeps track of the dates that cost money or worse to miss, like court dates, license renewals and benefit recertifications, and sends the kind of plan-ahead reminder that New York City tested.
fixes.firstStep: Tell us you’d use this, and list the three deadlines this year that would cost you most to miss.

proc-saving-starts-automatically.title: Retirement savings that start without my signing up
proc-saving-starts-automatically.line: My retirement savings began on my first day at work, without my ever having to fill out the form I’d have put off.

fixes.title: Ask your employer to enroll new hires automatically
fixes.whatChanges: In a study first issued in 2000, the economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea found that at one large American company, enrolling new hires in the 401(k) plan unless they opted out raised sign-ups sharply. Most people stayed at the default contribution rate, so the default matters a lot.
fixes.firstStep: Ask HR whether new hires are enrolled in the retirement plan automatically, and at what rate.

fixes.title: Check whether you’re enrolled in your workplace plan
fixes.whatChanges: Signing up for a 401(k) is the kind of form many people mean to fill out and never do, which is why Madrian and Shea’s finding was so large. Checking takes a few minutes on most benefits sites.
fixes.firstStep: Log in to your benefits site or ask HR whether you’re enrolled, and write down your contribution rate.
